discovery.question: Your uncle warns you not to sleep in a closed room full of potted plants because 'plants start breathing at night.' A friend says that's nonsense. Who is closer to the truth?
options: Your uncle is half-right: plants take in oxygen day AND night — but in daylight photosynthesis masks it
Your uncle is fully right: plants photosynthesise by day and only respire at night
Your friend is right: plants never use oxygen at all
Neither — plants stop all gas exchange when they sleep
discovery.answer: Your uncle is half-right: plants take in oxygen day AND night — but in daylight photosynthesis masks it
discovery.hook: Plants don't flip a switch at sunset. Every living cell — even a root cell underground — respires around the clock. Sunlight only adds photosynthesis on top of it.

c10_bio_ch01.mission: Take one molecule of glucose from a morning paratha and escort it through digestion, the bloodstream, and a sprinting muscle cell until it becomes usable energy — then trace where its waste goes.
c10_bio_ch01.finale: Nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion are not four separate chapters in your body — they are one relay team. Drop any one of them and the whole system fails.
c10_bio_ch01.subtitle: Trace food to energy, and find out what your body throws out and why
c10_bio_ch01.role: a sports physiologist figuring out what fuels a sprinter
c10_bio_ch01.intro: A student eats an aloo paratha at 7:30 and is cycling hard by 8:00. Somewhere between the plate and the leg muscles, four life processes are working in perfect relay.
c10_bio_ch01.goal: Explain how the four life processes interlock, and never again confuse excretion with simply removing undigested food.

discovery.question: You touch a hot tawa and your hand yanks back — before you even feel the burn. Who actually gave the order to pull back?
options: The spinal cord, via a reflex arc — the 'feel the pain' signal reaches the brain a moment later
The brain, after it fully processes the pain
The skin cells, which push the hand away themselves
A hormone rushed to the arm muscles
discovery.answer: The spinal cord, via a reflex arc — the 'feel the pain' signal reaches the brain a moment later
discovery.hook: Your body doesn't wait for the brain on emergencies. Reflexes shortcut through the spinal cord — that's why you escape the burn before you can even describe it.

c10_bio_ch02.mission: Race a nerve impulse from a fingertip to a muscle — name every structure it crosses — then figure out how a touch-me-not plant folds its leaves with no nerves at all.
c10_bio_ch02.finale: Animals wire signals through neurons; plants do it with slow chemical and electrical waves. Different hardware, same job: sense the world, respond fast enough to survive.
c10_bio_ch02.subtitle: Chase a signal through neurons, hormones and a folding mimosa leaf
c10_bio_ch02.role: an emergency-response coordinator inside a living body
c10_bio_ch02.intro: A finger meets a hot pan; a mimosa leaf snaps shut at a touch. Both are responses to a stimulus — but the machinery underneath could not be more different.
c10_bio_ch02.goal: Map the full stimulus-to-response pathway and explain how plants coordinate without a nervous system.

discovery.question: A farmer clones one amazingly sweet strawberry plant using runners. Five years later a single fungus wipes out the entire crop in one season. What made the crop so fragile?
options: Every plant was genetically identical, so a disease that beat one plant beat them all
The fungus only attacks strawberries that taste sweet
Runners physically carried the fungus between fields
Cloned plants simply die after five years
discovery.answer: Every plant was genetically identical, so a disease that beat one plant beat them all
discovery.hook: Asexual reproduction is fast and faithful — but 'faithful' means zero variety. When every plant has the same defences, one germ becomes a species-wide disaster.

c10_bio_ch03.mission: Compare Amoeba splitting in two, a potato sprouting from 'eyes', and a seed formed after pollination — then decide which strategy you'd bet a species on.
c10_bio_ch03.finale: Reproduction doesn't keep you alive — it keeps your species alive. The real drama is the trade-off: copy yourself perfectly and fast, or shuffle the genes and gamble on variation.
c10_bio_ch03.subtitle: From splitting amoebas to sprouting potatoes — how life makes more life
c10_bio_ch03.role: an agricultural scientist protecting a crop from collapse
c10_bio_ch03.intro: A mango tree drops seeds; a potato on your shelf grows eyes and becomes a whole new plant. Same goal — wildly different machinery.
c10_bio_ch03.goal: Distinguish asexual from sexual reproduction and explain why variation is a survival strategy, not a side effect.

discovery.question: A pure tall pea plant is crossed with a pure dwarf one. Every single offspring grows tall. Then those offspring are self-pollinated — and dwarf plants reappear, about one in four. Where was 'dwarf' hiding?
options: In the F1 plants' cells — each carried a hidden recessive allele that resurfaced when gametes combined
In the soil — dwarfism was caused by nutrients, not genes
Nowhere — the second generation mutated back to dwarf
In the pollen of neighbouring dwarf plants that contaminated the cross
discovery.answer: In the F1 plants' cells — each carried a hidden recessive allele that resurfaced when gametes combined
discovery.hook: Traits don't blend or vanish. A recessive allele can sit silent in a tall plant for a whole generation and still come back in the next — that's the famous 3:1.

c10_bio_ch04.mission: Run Mendel's crosses yourself: predict F1 and F2 for contrasting traits, then work out why two siblings from the same parents never look identical.
c10_bio_ch04.finale: Heredity is a card shuffle, not a photocopy. Segregation, independent assortment and a little mutation mean every generation is a brand-new deal.
c10_bio_ch04.subtitle: Predict traits like Mendel and explain why siblings differ
c10_bio_ch04.role: a plant breeder choosing which seeds to sow
c10_bio_ch04.intro: Plant tall peas next to dwarf ones and the maths of inheritance appears in your garden — clean ratios hiding a deeper machinery of alleles.
c10_bio_ch04.goal: Predict monohybrid cross outcomes, read a Punnett square, and name the real sources of variation.

discovery.question: Purple potassium permanganate dropped in water turns the whole glass purple. A classmate calls it a chemical change 'because the colour changed.' What's the verdict?
options: Physical change — the molecules spread out but stay exactly the same substance
Chemical change — any colour change proves a new substance formed
Chemical change — because the change cannot be reversed by hand
Neither — dissolving isn't a change at all
discovery.answer: Physical change — the molecules spread out but stay exactly the same substance
discovery.hook: Colour change is a clue, not a verdict. A chemical change needs a NEW substance — gas, precipitate, heat — not just a new look.

c10_chem_ch01.mission: Play chemical detective: catch the signs of a real reaction, write it as an equation, and balance it — without ever touching a subscript.
c10_chem_ch01.finale: An equation is a promise: the atoms you start with are the atoms you end with. Coefficients keep the books balanced; subscripts would rewrite the substance itself.
c10_chem_ch01.subtitle: Spot real chemical change and balance the story atom by atom
c10_chem_ch01.role: a forensic chemist reading evidence at a reaction scene
c10_chem_ch01.intro: Limescale fizzes under vinegar, magnesium burns with a blinding flash, and a purple crystal quietly dissolves. Some of these are new substances being born — some are not.
c10_chem_ch01.goal: Identify chemical change by its observable signs and write balanced equations using coefficients only.

discovery.question: A yellow turmeric stain on a white kurta turns reddish-brown the moment it meets soap water. Your friend says the soap 'bleached the colour.' What's really happening?
options: Turmeric is a natural indicator — it turns reddish-brown in the soap's basic solution
The soap bleached the turmeric dye, same as it removes grease
Heat from the water burnt the stain darker
Turmeric reacted with the fabric, not the soap
discovery.answer: Turmeric is a natural indicator — it turns reddish-brown in the soap's basic solution
discovery.hook: Your kitchen is full of hidden pH meters. Turmeric, litmus, phenolphthalein — they flip colour depending on H⁺ versus OH⁻, and the kitchen chemistry gives it away.

c10_chem_ch02.mission: Identify three unlabelled solutions using only litmus and phenolphthalein, then explain why magnesium fizzes violently in one acid but lazily in another at the same concentration.
c10_chem_ch02.finale: Acids and bases aren't about being 'dangerous' or 'safe' — they're about ions. Strength is how fully a substance lets go of them, and indicators make that invisible tug visible.
c10_chem_ch02.subtitle: Unmask mystery solutions with indicators and decode acid strength
c10_chem_ch02.role: a quality-control chemist in a food-testing lab
c10_chem_ch02.intro: Lemon on a cut stings; baking soda calms heartburn. Behind both is the same quiet tug-of-war between hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions.
c10_chem_ch02.goal: Use indicators correctly — including the ones that trick students — and explain acid strength as degree of ionisation.

discovery.question: A pencil 'lead' completes a circuit and the LED glows. A classmate declares: 'It conducts, so graphite must be a metal.' Your move?
options: Graphite is a non-metal that conducts — its delocalised electrons are a famous exception
He's right — anything that conducts electricity is a metal
It's neither — pencil lead isn't really carbon
Graphite conducts only because of clay mixed into the pencil
discovery.answer: Graphite is a non-metal that conducts — its delocalised electrons are a famous exception
discovery.hook: One property never defines a class. Mercury is a liquid metal; graphite is a conducting non-metal; diamond is a non-metal harder than any steel. Check the whole profile.

c10_chem_ch03.mission: Given three mystery samples — a slippery black conductor, a brittle yellow powder, a shiny grey liquid — identify each and justify the call with properties, not guesses.
c10_chem_ch03.finale: Metals shine, bend and conduct because of how their electrons pool; non-metals break the pattern wherever bonding allows it. Learn the reasons and the exceptions stop being exceptions.
c10_chem_ch03.subtitle: Sort metals from non-metals — including the ones that break the rules
c10_chem_ch03.role: a materials engineer picking metals for real jobs
c10_chem_ch03.intro: A goldsmith hammers a sheet thinner than paper, an electrician pulls copper wire, and a pencil somehow lights an LED. One property at a time, the periodic table starts making sense.
c10_chem_ch03.goal: Link metallic properties to electron behaviour and handle the classic exceptions — graphite, mercury, diamond — without flinching.

discovery.question: A diamond and a pencil tip are both 100% pure carbon. One is the hardest natural substance and can't conduct; the other is soft, slippery, and lights an LED. How can identical atoms produce opposites?
options: The carbon atoms are bonded in different 3-D networks — bonding pattern, not atom type, sets the properties
Diamond has hidden impurities that make it hard
Graphite is partly metallic, which is why it conducts
Diamond is older, so its atoms had time to harden
discovery.answer: The carbon atoms are bonded in different 3-D networks — bonding pattern, not atom type, sets the properties
discovery.hook: Carbon's superpower isn't the atom — it's the architecture. Share electrons four ways in a rigid lattice and you get diamond; in sliding sheets and you get graphite.

c10_chem_ch04.mission: Build carbon's molecules yourself: draw electron-dot structures that respect tetravalency, then hunt down every structural isomer hiding inside C₅H₁₂.
c10_chem_ch04.finale: Four bonds plus the ability to chain with itself — that's how one element fills the world with petrol, plastic, cotton, medicine and you.
c10_chem_ch04.subtitle: Draw, branch and count the millions of shapes carbon can take
c10_chem_ch04.role: an organic chemist sketching never-before-seen molecules
c10_chem_ch04.intro: The gas in your stove, the vinegar in your kitchen and the cotton on your back are all carbon compounds — held together by one quiet rule: share, don't steal, electrons.
c10_chem_ch04.goal: Draw correct electron-dot structures, apply tetravalency, and explain catenation and isomerism.

discovery.question: Take lithium (7), sodium (23) and potassium (39). Sodium's mass, 23, is almost exactly the average of 7 and 39 — and all three metals behave alike. Coincidence?
options: No — it's a real pattern: Dobereiner found triads where the middle element's mass averages the other two
Yes — atomic mass has nothing to do with chemical behaviour
No — but only because all three are stored in oil
It's a coincidence that works for these three but for no other elements
discovery.answer: No — it's a real pattern: Dobereiner found triads where the middle element's mass averages the other two
discovery.hook: Before the periodic table existed, chemists were already hearing its rhythm — threes that averaged out, then eighths that repeated. The table was discovered by listening for patterns.

c10_chem_ch05.mission: Rebuild classification history: test Dobereiner's triads, lay out Newlands' octaves, and find the exact elements where each scheme breaks.
c10_chem_ch05.finale: Every failed scheme taught chemists something. Triads showed mass patterns, octaves showed repetition — and their failures cleared the road for Mendeleev's leap.
c10_chem_ch05.subtitle: Hunt the number patterns that predicted the periodic table
c10_chem_ch05.role: a 19th-century chemist racing to organise the elements
c10_chem_ch05.intro: Fifty-six known elements, no table, no order — just scattered facts. Your job: find the hidden rhythm that makes similar elements fall into place.
c10_chem_ch05.goal: State Dobereiner's and Newlands' rules precisely — atomic weight, not atomic number — and pinpoint where each fails.

discovery.question: Belgium ran 541 days with NO elected government — yet salaries were paid, courts sat, schools stayed open. Sri Lanka had a rock-solid majority government — and slid into civil war. What did Belgium get right?
options: It divided power so no community could be steamrolled — regions and community governments kept everyone inside the system
It had richer citizens who didn't need a government
Its army kept order while politicians argued
It got lucky — 541 days was a fluke, not a design
discovery.answer: It divided power so no community could be steamrolled — regions and community governments kept everyone inside the system
discovery.hook: Majority rule without accommodation is a slow-burning fuse. Belgium rewrote its constitution four times to share power; Sri Lanka let one community hoard it — and paid with a war.

c10_civ_ch01.mission: Take a city split 60-40 between two language groups and design a power-sharing deal — then stress-test it against what happened in Sri Lanka.
c10_civ_ch01.finale: Power sharing isn't weakness — it's the load-bearing wall of a diverse country. Belgium proves a state can pause its government without breaking; Sri Lanka proves the alternative.
c10_civ_ch01.subtitle: Compare two countries that answered 'who rules?' very differently
c10_civ_ch01.role: a constitutional designer for a divided nation
c10_civ_ch01.intro: One country speaks Dutch and French; another is Sinhalese and Tamil. Both had to answer the same question: can the majority simply take everything?
c10_civ_ch01.goal: Contrast accommodation with majoritarianism and explain why sharing power is prudential AND moral.

discovery.question: India's Centre can redraw a state's borders without asking it (Article 3) and can take over a state in an emergency. A student concludes: 'India is secretly a unitary country.' Is she right?
options: No — states have constitutionally guaranteed subjects the Centre can't touch, and courts referee the divide
Yes — if the Centre can override states, federalism is just decoration
Only during emergencies — otherwise India is fully federal
Half-right — India was federal until the 42nd Amendment ended it
discovery.answer: No — states have constitutionally guaranteed subjects the Centre can't touch, and courts referee the divide
discovery.hook: Federalism isn't equal power — it's guaranteed power. India tilts toward the Centre, but the Seventh Schedule draws lines even Parliament can't casually cross.

c10_civ_ch02.mission: Sort real subjects into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists, then referee a Centre-versus-State clash and rule who wins — and why.
c10_civ_ch02.finale: Two levels of government, one citizen, zero ambiguity — that's the federal bargain. When the lists collide, the Constitution and the courts settle it, not muscle.
c10_civ_ch02.subtitle: Referee the tug-of-war between the Centre and the states
c10_civ_ch02.role: a constitutional advisor to the Supreme Court
c10_civ_ch02.intro: The Delhi Metro is run by the Centre; the school down the road by the state; your panchayat by the village. Who decided that — and who decides when they fight?
c10_civ_ch02.goal: Explain the three-list division of powers, residuary subjects, and why India's federalism is asymmetric but real.

discovery.question: Riya and Rahul are both software engineers working nine hours a day. At home, Riya does 100% of the cooking, cleaning and childcare — and the family praises her for 'managing so well.' What's actually going on?
options: Sexual division of labour — her paid job is visible, her second unpaid shift at home is treated as natural
Nothing — she simply enjoys housework more than Rahul
A fair split — equal office hours means equal total work
A private family choice that no concept can describe
discovery.answer: Sexual division of labour — her paid job is visible, her second unpaid shift at home is treated as natural
discovery.hook: The trick is calling it 'natural.' Once housework is labelled a woman's duty, her double burden stops looking like inequality — and starts looking like praise.

c10_civ_ch03.mission: Audit one day in a household: log every task, tag who does it and whether it's paid — then expose where the 'public' world ends and the invisible 'private' workload begins.
c10_civ_ch03.finale: Politics doesn't stop at the doorstep. The public-private divide decides whose work counts as work — and feminism's demand is simple: count all of it, share all of it.
c10_civ_ch03.subtitle: Expose the unpaid second shift hiding inside 'normal' family life
c10_civ_ch03.role: a social researcher measuring work that never appears in GDP
c10_civ_ch03.intro: A mother nurses patients all day, then cooks dinner while everyone watches TV — and calls it duty. Your job is to make the invisible work visible.
c10_civ_ch03.goal: Define sexual division of labour and the public-private divide, and connect them to women's political participation.

discovery.question: TMC runs the government of West Bengal — yet the Election Commission revoked its 'national party' status, while AAP, newer and smaller, got it. How can a party that rules a whole state lose that tag?
options: 'National' is an election-performance label — vote share and seats across several states — not a measure of governing power
It can't — the Election Commission made an obvious error
AAP bribed its way to the status; TMC refused to
TMC lost it because it only contests state elections, never Lok Sabha
discovery.answer: 'National' is an election-performance label — vote share and seats across several states — not a measure of governing power
discovery.hook: The tag sounds like prestige but it's pure arithmetic: roughly 6% of valid votes in four-plus states and at least four Lok Sabha seats. Governing a state doesn't enter the formula.

c10_civ_ch04.mission: Play Election Commissioner: apply the official criteria to real parties, decide who earns the national tag — and explain why democracy can't run without parties at all.
c10_civ_ch04.finale: Parties are how 968 million voters' clashing preferences get bundled into a governable choice. Visible at election time, indispensable every day in between.
c10_civ_ch04.subtitle: Crack the criteria that make a party 'national' — and why parties exist
c10_civ_ch04.role: an Election Commission official auditing party status
c10_civ_ch04.intro: Symbols on TV, manifestos in the news, governments rising and falling — parties are democracy's loudest institutions. But what exactly earns one the word 'national'?
c10_civ_ch04.goal: State the ECI criteria for national-party status and list what parties do between elections, not just during them.

discovery.question: From 1950 to 2000, dictatorships averaged 4.42% growth a year while democracies averaged 3.95%. Case closed for dictatorship — right?
options: No — dictatorships swung wildly between booms and collapses, while democracies grew slower but never crashed into famine
Yes — a higher average growth rate settles the debate
No — the data is too old to mean anything today
Yes — but only for countries that were already rich
discovery.answer: No — dictatorships swung wildly between booms and collapses, while democracies grew slower but never crashed into famine
discovery.hook: The average hides the horror. Half a point of growth buys you stability, dignity and no catastrophic lows — development is more than a GDP line going up.

c10_civ_ch05.mission: Judge two countries: one dictatorial with 8% growth but 65% literacy, one democratic at 5% with 92% literacy — build the case for which is truly more 'developed.'
c10_civ_ch05.finale: Democracy's report card isn't only economic — it's accountability, dignity and citizens who can demand answers. Growth matters; so does who the growth belongs to.
c10_civ_ch05.subtitle: Weigh growth numbers against dignity, rights and real development
c10_civ_ch05.role: a development economist comparing national report cards
c10_civ_ch05.intro: A scholarship stuck in a government office gets released within 30 days of an RTI filing. That small win is accountability — one of democracy's quieter outcomes.
c10_civ_ch05.goal: Distinguish growth from development and argue democracy's outcomes — accountability, legitimacy, dignity — with evidence.

discovery.question: A mining company offers a tribal district roads, schools and jobs. The Gram Sabha rejects it to protect their forest and way of life. Who understands 'development' correctly?
options: Both — development means different things to different people, and their goals can genuinely clash
Only the company — roads and jobs are real development, forests are sentimental
Only the Gram Sabha — development always means refusing industry
Neither — development has one fixed definition that settles this
discovery.answer: Both — development means different things to different people, and their goals can genuinely clash
discovery.hook: There is no single scoreboard for a good life. A wage, a forest, a safe walk to school — what counts as 'developed' depends on whose life you're measuring.

c10_eco_ch01.mission: Interview four people in a village — a landless labourer, a farmer, a schoolgirl, a factory owner — and prove their versions of 'development' can't all be bought with the same rupee.
c10_eco_ch01.finale: Income is a means, not the destination. Real development is a bundle of goals — freedom, equality, security — that sometimes even collide with each other.
c10_eco_ch01.subtitle: Discover why 'a better life' means different things to different people
c10_eco_ch01.role: a panchayat advisor deciding how to spend a development fund
c10_eco_ch01.intro: A district gets money for exactly one project — a watershed, a skill centre, or a cold storage. Every group in the village wants a different one, and each has a point.
c10_eco_ch01.goal: Explain that development goals vary and conflict, and separate income goals from freedom, equality and security.

discovery.question: A sugar mill buys sugarcane straight from farmers. Since it works on a primary-sector crop, the mill must be primary sector too — right?
options: Wrong — the mill transforms cane into sugar, so it's secondary; it's the output, not the input, that decides the sector
Right — anything using farm produce stays in the primary sector
It's tertiary — because the mill also sells the sugar
It splits — half primary for crushing, half secondary for packing
discovery.answer: Wrong — the mill transforms cane into sugar, so it's secondary; it's the output, not the input, that decides the sector
discovery.hook: Don't classify a job by what goes in — classify it by what comes out. Nature's gift is primary, a transformed thing is secondary, a service is tertiary.

c10_eco_ch02.mission: Trace one litre of milk from a cow in a village to a chilled packet in a city store — tag every stage primary, secondary or tertiary — then explain why services rule India's GDP but not its jobs.
c10_eco_ch02.finale: Wheat to flour to a delivered pizza: one grain, three sectors. India's puzzle is that the sector earning the most isn't the one employing the most.
c10_eco_ch02.subtitle: Sort the whole economy into three buckets — then find the imbalance
c10_eco_ch02.role: an economist mapping India's production chain
c10_eco_ch02.intro: Your grandfather's village grows the wheat; a mill grinds it; a delivery app brings the pizza. Every rupee you spend lands in one of three sectors.
c10_eco_ch02.goal: Classify activities by nature of output and analyse why tertiary leads GDP while primary still leads employment.

discovery.question: A wheat farmer needs shoes. In a barter world, what must happen before he can trade?
options: He must find a shoemaker who wants wheat, in the right amount, right now — a double coincidence of wants
He just needs to find any shoemaker with his shoe size
He needs the government to fix a wheat-for-shoes rate
Nothing special — barter works exactly like money
discovery.answer: He must find a shoemaker who wants wheat, in the right amount, right now — a double coincidence of wants
discovery.hook: Barter doesn't just make trade awkward — it makes whole industries impossible. Money's real job is letting you sell to one person and buy from another.

c10_eco_ch03.mission: Sell 50 kg of tomatoes, survive a barter nightmare, then track your own salary through cash, UPI and deposits to see what actually counts as 'money.'
c10_eco_ch03.finale: A ₹500 note and a UPI balance are both money — one printed and guaranteed, the other a promise your bank keeps on demand. Money is trust you can spend.
c10_eco_ch03.subtitle: From barter chaos to UPI — what makes money, money
c10_eco_ch03.role: a village trader trying to escape the barter trap
c10_eco_ch03.intro: In a remote haat, a trader can't sell his cloth because the farmers don't want what he brought. One invention would fix it — and you carry it in your pocket.
c10_eco_ch03.goal: Explain double coincidence of wants, and treat demand deposits as real money alongside currency.

discovery.question: Your phone was 'assembled in India' — yet its processor was designed in the USA, chips came from Korea, the screen from China. So which country actually made your phone?
options: No single country — a global production chain splits each stage wherever it's cheapest or most skilled
China — because most parts shipped from there
India — because final assembly is where a product is 'made'
The USA — because the company that designed it is American
discovery.answer: No single country — a global production chain splits each stage wherever it's cheapest or most skilled
discovery.hook: Globalisation isn't about importing finished goods — it's about slicing one product across the planet so each piece is made where it makes most sense.

c10_eco_ch04.mission: Follow an electric scooter's battery, body and assembly across three countries, compute the landed cost of imported wheat, and judge who wins when markets integrate.
c10_eco_ch04.finale: One product, many passports. MNCs stitch the world into a single factory — and the fight is over who captures the value and who gets just the wages.
c10_eco_ch04.subtitle: Unpick the global journey of the products in your pocket
c10_eco_ch04.role: a trade analyst mapping where products really come from
c10_eco_ch04.intro: Samsung, Apple, Xiaomi and Lava all fight for space on one Indian shelf — a sight impossible when import duties topped 100% and two car models ruled the roads.
c10_eco_ch04.goal: Explain global production chains and market integration, including why prices converge but never fully equalise.

discovery.question: A ₹500 'pure ghee' packet turns out adulterated. The shopkeeper blames the company, the company ignores your letter, and a lawyer costs more than the ghee. What does this prove?
options: Individual buyers are too weak to fight alone — that's exactly why a consumer movement had to be organised
Nothing — cheating on small purchases is just part of shopping
Only expensive products deserve legal protection
The consumer should simply stop buying branded goods
discovery.answer: Individual buyers are too weak to fight alone — that's exactly why a consumer movement had to be organised
discovery.hook: One cheated buyer is a nuisance; a movement is a force. The rights you now take for granted were won by two decades of testing, exposing and organising.

c10_eco_ch05.mission: Take a burst pressure cooker with no ISI mark and no refund to the District Forum — identify every right violated and argue for the relief a consumer deserves.
c10_eco_ch05.finale: Safety, information, choice, redressal — four rights that turned 'buyer beware' into 'seller, be fair.' The movement started long before the law caught up.
c10_eco_ch05.subtitle: Turn a bad purchase into a case the law must answer
c10_eco_ch05.role: a consumer-rights advocate arguing before a district forum
c10_eco_ch05.intro: A pressure cooker lid bursts on first use — no instructions, no ISI mark, no refund. What sounds like bad luck is actually four legal violations at once.
c10_eco_ch05.goal: Name the consumer rights, trace the movement that won them, and apply them to real complaints.

discovery.question: Lencho's crops are destroyed, so he writes a letter addressed simply 'To God' demanding 100 pesos. When the post office staff collect 70 and send it, he's angry — not grateful. What does his anger reveal?
options: His faith was so literal he believed God sent the full amount — and the post office 'stole' the rest
He's ungrateful — 70 pesos should have been enough
He realised too late that writing to God was foolish
He was angry the letter took so long to deliver
discovery.answer: His faith was so literal he believed God sent the full amount — and the post office 'stole' the rest
discovery.hook: Lencho isn't a fool — he's a man with no bank, no insurance, no helpline. When no human institution will help, absolute faith in God is the only plan left.

c10_engl_ch01.mission: Reread the hailstorm scene and hunt the imagery — 'frozen pearls,' a field 'white as if covered with salt' — then build a PEEL answer on what Lencho's faith really is.
c10_engl_ch01.finale: The story's deepest irony: the people who answered his letter proved his faith in God — while he accused them of robbing him. Faith and irony share one envelope.
c10_engl_ch01.subtitle: Read a letter to God and the irony of the humans who answered it
c10_engl_ch01.role: a literary detective decoding what a farmer's letter really means
c10_engl_ch01.intro: A farmer loses everything to one hour of hail, and his solution is a stamp, a pen and an address no post office can deliver.
c10_engl_ch01.goal: Analyse Lencho's faith as literal and transactional, and support every claim with textual evidence.

discovery.question: At Mandela's 1994 inauguration, the military generals who once would have arrested him now saluted him — and two national anthems played, one for each community. Why sing BOTH anthems?
options: It was a deliberate act of reconciliation — no group's identity was erased in the new nation
It was just ceremony — extra songs to fill the program
The organisers couldn't decide which anthem to keep
One anthem was for Mandela, the other for the outgoing president
discovery.answer: It was a deliberate act of reconciliation — no group's identity was erased in the new nation
discovery.hook: That day wasn't only about one man's freedom — it was a whole country performing a new idea: that the oppressor and the oppressed could belong to the same anthem.

c10_engl_ch02.mission: Reconstruct the machinery of apartheid — the acts that assigned race, controlled movement, and dictated where people could exist — then weigh what the inauguration dismantled.
c10_engl_ch02.finale: Apartheid wasn't just separate benches; it was a legal machine that defined who you were at birth. Freedom meant dismantling the machine, not just opening the benches.
c10_engl_ch02.subtitle: Walk out of apartheid's cage into a rainbow nation's first morning
c10_engl_ch02.role: a journalist covering 10 May 1994 at the Union Buildings
c10_engl_ch02.intro: For decades your skin decided your school, your bench, your bus. On one May morning in Pretoria, that entire system bowed to a man it had imprisoned for 27 years.
c10_engl_ch02.goal: Explain apartheid as a legal-bureaucratic system and read the inauguration as a national ritual of reconciliation.

discovery.question: The young seagull's mother flies up with a piece of fish — then halts mid-air, just out of his reach. Starving, he dives at the fish and finds himself flying. Was the family abandoning him all along?
options: No — they staged a controlled crisis: withholding food, circling, calling, until hunger beat fear
Yes — they gave up on him and left him to survive or starve
No — the mother simply couldn't land on the narrow ledge
Partly — they abandoned him but came back when they heard him cry
discovery.answer: No — they staged a controlled crisis: withholding food, circling, calling, until hunger beat fear
discovery.hook: The first flight wasn't bravery — it was engineering. His family built a situation where staying afraid cost more than jumping.

c10_engl_ch03.mission: Track every detail the author plants — the mocking siblings, the hunger, the mother hovering with fish — and argue whether the seagull conquered fear or fear was outmanoeuvred.
c10_engl_ch03.finale: Sometimes the only way past a ledge is a push you don't recognise as love. Hunger did what courage couldn't — and the sea caught him gently.
c10_engl_ch03.subtitle: Watch a terrified seagull get tricked into his first flight
c10_engl_ch03.role: a behavioural scientist reading a bird family's strategy
c10_engl_ch03.intro: His brothers and sister flew days ago. He watches from the ledge, pretending to sleep, too scared to try — until his mother weaponises his own stomach.
c10_engl_ch03.goal: Analyse fear as layered psychology and support claims about the family's deliberate staging with evidence.

discovery.question: Anne Frank writes 'Dear Kitty' instead of 'Dear Diary,' and says 'paper has more patience than people.' In a sealed-off annex, what is the diary actually doing for her?
options: It's a survival tool — writing builds her a confidante and a self that the Nazis were trying to erase
It's a teenage phase — she's just a normal lonely girl who wants a friend
It's homework — she planned to publish it as a book someday
It's evidence — she was recording Nazi crimes for a future trial
discovery.answer: It's a survival tool — writing builds her a confidante and a self that the Nazis were trying to erase
discovery.hook: When a regime strips you of your school, your tram, your park bench — writing 'I still exist' onto a page is not a hobby. It's resistance.

c10_engl_ch04.mission: Place a 13-year-old's diary inside its history — trace the laws that caged her life — then prove why 'lonely teenager' is a one-mark answer, not a three-mark one.
c10_engl_ch04.finale: The Holocaust isn't background to the diary — it's the lens for every entry. Anne wrote in real time, not knowing the ending, which is exactly why we can't stop reading.
c10_engl_ch04.subtitle: Meet the girl who turned a notebook into a lifeline
c10_engl_ch04.role: a historian reading a real-time document of the Holocaust
c10_engl_ch04.intro: Forbidden from trams, schools and park benches at thirteen, a girl in hiding names her diary and tells it everything she cannot tell a soul.
c10_engl_ch04.goal: Connect the diary to Holocaust history and explain Kitty as confidante, not literary device.

discovery.question: In a Goan village, a man in a knee-length kabai arrives each morning to the 'jhang-jhang' of a bamboo staff — and the text insists he is NOT a relic of the past. What is he really?
options: A living cultural institution — his breads are still essential to every Goan festival and marriage
A quaint historical figure — the last of the old Portuguese bakers
Just a bread-seller doing his morning and evening rounds
A tourist attraction maintained for nostalgia
discovery.answer: A living cultural institution — his breads are still essential to every Goan festival and marriage
discovery.hook: The pader didn't survive as a museum piece. Bol at Christmas, sandwiches at engagements — Goa took a Portuguese import and made it impossible to celebrate without.

c10_engl_ch05.mission: Follow the baker's daily route through the village — his kabai, his furnace, his jhang-jhang — and show how a colonial legacy became a Goan necessity.
c10_engl_ch05.finale: Culture isn't what invaders leave behind; it's what people choose to keep. The pader endures because Goa kneaded Portuguese bread into its own identity.
c10_engl_ch05.subtitle: Hear the jhang-jhang that still runs a Goan village's mornings
c10_engl_ch05.role: a food historian tracing how bread became Goan
c10_engl_ch05.intro: Before alarm clocks, a bamboo staff's rhythm told a Goan village that morning — and fresh pao — had arrived.
c10_engl_ch05.goal: Explain the Portuguese legacy in Goan baking and why the pader is a cultural institution, not a vendor.

discovery.question: After his dog Jonnie dies, Maxwell doesn't get another dog — he imports an otter from Iraq. A classmate says: 'He was lonely and otters are cute.' What's missing from that reading?
options: A deliberate chain of reasoning — grief, rejecting a replacement dog, a childhood fascination, and a cottage ringed by water fit for an otter
Nothing — loneliness fully explains an impulse purchase
Money — only a rich man could order an otter
Luck — an otter happened to be available nearby
discovery.answer: A deliberate chain of reasoning — grief, rejecting a replacement dog, a childhood fascination, and a cottage ringed by water fit for an otter
discovery.hook: Mijbil wasn't a whim; he was a decision with steps. And his settling in wasn't a straight line — joy one day, panic the next, like any wild thing learning a house.

c10_engl_ch06.mission: Chart Mijbil's first days — the hiding, the bathroom experiments, the glorious chaos in water — and show why 'he adapted quickly' only earns half the marks.
c10_engl_ch06.finale: A wild animal doesn't 'settle'; it negotiates. Maxwell's patience and Mijbil's zig-zag trust are the real story of two species learning each other.
c10_engl_ch06.subtitle: Track an otter's zig-zag road from Iraqi marshes to a Scottish home
c10_engl_ch06.role: an animal behaviourist observing a wild otter indoors
c10_engl_ch06.intro: A remote cottage by the water, a man grieving his dog, and a parcel from Iraq containing something that would turn bathtubs into playgrounds.
c10_engl_ch06.goal: Trace Maxwell's decision-making and Mijbil's non-linear adaptation using concrete behavioural evidence.

discovery.question: Eight-year-old Valli rides the bus to town and back — alone. She never does chores for cash, never asks the conductor directly. So how did she pull it off?
options: Months of resisting peppermints and toys to save sixty paise — plus fare and timing details lifted from eavesdropping
She saved gift money and boldly questioned the driver about the route
She snuck aboard while the conductor was distracted
Her mother secretly funded the trip as a surprise
discovery.answer: Months of resisting peppermints and toys to save sixty paise — plus fare and timing details lifted from eavesdropping
discovery.hook: This isn't childish daydreaming — it's a project. Every coin refused, every adult conversation mined for clues. Valli planned her ride like a heist.

c10_engl_ch07.mission: Piece together Valli's intelligence operation — what she overheard, what she sacrificed, what she refused — then write the case for her 'tiny wish' being iron will.
c10_engl_ch07.finale: The bus was never the point — the self-control was. An eight-year-old who can resist a hundred peppermints can get almost anywhere.
c10_engl_ch07.subtitle: Follow an eight-year-old's master plan for one bus ride
c10_engl_ch07.role: a biographer reconstructing how a child out-planned the adults
c10_engl_ch07.intro: Every day a bright bus roars past Valli's house toward a town she's never seen. Most kids would whine for a ride. Valli starts gathering intelligence instead.
c10_engl_ch07.goal: Show how the author builds character through indirect detail — observation, sacrifice, discretion — not just plot.

discovery.question: Kisa Gotami carries her dead son door to door begging for medicine. The neighbours say she's lost her senses. Are they being cruel — or seeing something she can't?
options: They're seeing grief's blindness — her love is so total it overrides the plain fact that he's gone
They're cruel — a good neighbour would search for the medicine with her
Neither — they simply didn't have any medicine to give
They're afraid — her grief might be contagious
discovery.answer: They're seeing grief's blindness — her love is so total it overrides the plain fact that he's gone
discovery.hook: The parable doesn't mock her — it honours her. Buddha's cure isn't medicine for the boy; it's a lesson that lets a shattered mother finally set him down.

c10_engl_ch08.mission: Trace Siddhartha's road from palace to the Bodhi tree — and don't mix up the Four Sights with the Four Noble Truths — then follow Kisa Gotami's mustard-seed journey.
c10_engl_ch08.finale: Every door she knocked had buried someone. That's the sermon without words: grief is universal, and accepting impermanence is the only medicine that exists.
c10_engl_ch08.subtitle: Walk from a prince's palace to a mother's unbearable lesson
c10_engl_ch08.role: a student of Buddha decoding a 2,500-year-old teaching
c10_engl_ch08.intro: A sheltered prince sees an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a monk — and abandons a kingdom. Years later, a grieving mother brings him her impossible request.
c10_engl_ch08.goal: Sequence the Buddha's transformation and interpret the mustard-seed parable as a lesson in universal mortality.

discovery.question: Lomov visits his neighbour to propose marriage — and the play ends with the 'engaged' couple screaming about whose dog is superior. What is Chekhov actually satirising?
options: People who prize winning arguments and property over the very marriage they're arranging
Romantic love — the play says all proposals end badly
Bad manners — the characters just needed etiquette lessons
Dogs — the real subject is which breed is best
discovery.answer: People who prize winning arguments and property over the very marriage they're arranging
discovery.hook: The proposal is bait, not the point. Chekhov makes the meadows worthless and the evidence vague on purpose — so you watch pride detonate over absolutely nothing.

c10_engl_ch09.mission: Dissect the Oxen Meadows quarrel line by line: find every ownership claim, notice how worthless the prize is, and explain why the argument is funniest precisely because it's pointless.
c10_engl_ch09.finale: A marriage proposal derailed by meadows and dogs isn't a rom-com — it's a farce holding up a mirror: watch what people fight for when nobody's watching their dignity.
c10_engl_ch09.subtitle: Watch a marriage proposal get demolished by a land dispute
c10_engl_ch09.role: a theatre critic reviewing a farce that refuses to be romantic
c10_engl_ch09.intro: A man in evening dress comes to propose. Before he can finish, he and the bride-to-be are shouting about a strip of land worth almost nothing.
c10_engl_ch09.goal: Identify the farce genre, analyse the Oxen Meadows argument, and correct the 'romantic comedy' misreading.

discovery.question: Mrs. Pumphrey feeds Tricki malt, cod-liver oil, Horlicks, cream cakes and chocolates because she believes he is weak and suffering. The vet, Mr. Herriot, takes Tricki away and gives him NO medicine at all — yet the dog recovers completely. What actually cured him?
options: A normal diet, exercise and play with other dogs — the 'illness' was overfeeding, not disease
A secret injection the vet hid from Mrs. Pumphrey
Being separated from his owner lowered his stress hormones
The surgery hinted at in the story's title
discovery.answer: A normal diet, exercise and play with other dogs — the 'illness' was overfeeding, not disease
discovery.hook: The 'triumph of surgery' is ironic — no surgery ever happens. Love expressed as unlimited treats made Tricki ill, and simple discipline cured him.

c10_engl_ch10.mission: Play the vet: examine an overweight, listless dog, separate real symptoms from an owner's anxious guesses, and design a recovery plan using only food, exercise and company.
c10_engl_ch10.finale: Pampering can be a slow-acting poison. Tricki didn't need medicine — he needed someone brave enough to say 'no more cream cakes.'
c10_engl_ch10.subtitle: Diagnose a dog whose only disease is too much love
c10_engl_ch10.role: a veterinary surgeon facing a pampered patient
c10_engl_ch10.intro: A wealthy lady arrives at your clinic in tears: her little dog refuses food, vomits, and can barely waddle. She insists he needs more nourishment. You suspect the opposite.
c10_engl_ch10.goal: Distinguish real illness from overindulgence, and explain why responsible care sometimes means withholding what a pet loves.

discovery.question: Hari Singh, a skilled 15-year-old thief, steals ₹600 from Anil — the one man who trusted him and was teaching him to read and write. Hours later he secretly returns the money. Why would a professional thief give back a successful theft?
options: He realised education and Anil's trust could change his life in ways stolen money never could
He was afraid the police had already been informed
The notes were wet and damaged, so they were worthless
He planned to steal a bigger amount later
discovery.answer: He realised education and Anil's trust could change his life in ways stolen money never could
discovery.hook: The most valuable thing Anil gave Hari wasn't money — it was being treated as someone worth teaching. Stealing from a man who trusted him cost more than ₹600.

c10_engl_ch11.mission: Step inside the mind of a boy who survives by lying: weigh the thrill of an easy theft against the slow reward of learning to write your own name, and decide what to do at the railway station.
c10_engl_ch11.finale: Trust turned out to be the thing Hari couldn't steal — he could only lose it or earn it. He chose to earn it.
c10_engl_ch11.subtitle: Decide what a thief does when someone finally trusts him
c10_engl_ch11.role: a young thief at a crossroads
c10_engl_ch11.intro: You are Hari Singh: charming, quick, and honest about only one thing — that you steal. Then you meet Anil, who hands you his money, his kitchen and his time without asking questions.
c10_engl_ch11.goal: Analyse how trust and education can reform where punishment cannot.

discovery.question: Secret agent Ausable is fat, speaks with an American accent, and lives in a gloomy hotel room — nothing like a film spy. When rival agent Max bursts in with a pistol, Ausable wins without firing a shot or throwing a punch. How?
options: He invents a balcony outside the window so convincingly that Max steps backwards into thin air
He secretly signals the police through his telephone
He offers Max double the money to switch sides
He uses a hidden trapdoor installed by French intelligence
discovery.answer: He invents a balcony outside the window so convincingly that Max steps backwards into thin air
discovery.hook: Ausable's weapon wasn't a gun — it was a believable lie told calmly. The story argues presence of mind beats physical strength and spy-movie glamour.

c10_engl_ch12.mission: You are an unimpressive-looking agent cornered by an armed intruder. Invent a detail so believable that your enemy defeats himself — while a knock at the door keeps raising the stakes.
c10_engl_ch12.finale: Max brought a pistol; Ausable brought a story. The story won, because a lie believed is stronger than a weapon feared.
c10_engl_ch12.subtitle: Outwit an armed spy using nothing but a made-up balcony
c10_engl_ch12.role: a secret agent who looks nothing like one
c10_engl_ch12.intro: A young writer named Fowler followed you all evening expecting mystery and danger — and got a damp hotel room instead. Then the door opens, and there's a man with a gun. Time to become interesting.
c10_engl_ch12.goal: Show how calm thinking and convincing detail can overturn a physically hopeless situation.

discovery.question: Horace Danby is a respectable locksmith who robs one safe a year to buy rare books. At Shotover Grange, a charming young woman catches him mid-robbery, sweet-talks him into opening the safe 'for her jewellery' — and he goes to prison while she walks free. What was the twist?
options: She was a fellow thief who tricked him into leaving his fingerprints all over the safe
She was an undercover police officer gathering evidence
She was the house owner's wife setting a trap for him
She hypnotised him into confessing to the owners
discovery.answer: She was a fellow thief who tricked him into leaving his fingerprints all over the safe
discovery.hook: The man who believed in 'honour among thieves' met a thief who didn't. His careful gloves came off the moment he trusted the wrong person.

c10_engl_ch13.mission: Plan a 'perfect' annual burglary as a meticulous, honest-in-public thief — then discover mid-heist that the most dangerous person in the house isn't carrying a weapon but a smile.
c10_engl_ch13.finale: Horace planned for locks, alarms and dogs — everything except another thief. Charm turned out to be the only safe he couldn't crack.
c10_engl_ch13.subtitle: Pull off a careful robbery, then lose it all to a better liar
c10_engl_ch13.role: a gentleman thief with a passion for rare books
c10_engl_ch13.intro: Once a year you stop being a respectable locksmith and become a careful, solitary burglar — not for greed, but for beautiful rare books. This year's job at Shotover Grange is going perfectly. Almost.
c10_engl_ch13.goal: Trace how a single misplaced trust undid months of meticulous planning, and weigh the irony of a thief being out-thieved.

discovery.question: Griffin discovers drugs that make the human body's refractive index match air — light passes through him, so he becomes invisible. But footprints appear in mud, snow shows his steps, and stolen food bulges visibly in his invisible stomach. What does this reveal about his 'perfect' power?
options: Invisibility hides the body, not its effects — he still leaves evidence wherever he goes
The drugs were imperfect and kept wearing off randomly
His power worked only in daylight, like a vampire reversed
He could only stay invisible while holding his breath
discovery.answer: Invisibility hides the body, not its effects — he still leaves evidence wherever he goes
discovery.hook: Griffin could vanish but could not hide his footprints, his breath in cold air, or the food inside him. Being unseen is not the same as being untraceable.

c10_engl_ch14.mission: Test a scientific breakthrough that bends light around a human body — then survive a winter night as an invisible man who still needs warmth, food and shelter, all of which give him away.
c10_engl_ch14.finale: Science gave Griffin a miracle, and he used it for arson and theft. The footprints in the snow were the honest part of him — the man remained visible in his choices.
c10_engl_ch14.subtitle: Become invisible — and learn why that solves nothing
c10_engl_ch14.intro: You have done what no physicist dreamed of: swallowed rare drugs, watched your body turn transparent as air. Then you step outside into a London January and realise the cold doesn't care that it can't see you.
c10_engl_ch14.goal: Explain the refractive-index logic of Griffin's invisibility and judge how a discovery's value depends on the hands that hold it.

discovery.question: Richard Ebright started as a kid collecting butterflies in Pennsylvania — his mother got him 'The Travels of Monarch X,' he tagged butterflies for research, and eventually his work helped explain how cells read DNA. What does his path reveal about how scientists are actually made?
options: Sustained curiosity plus real research habits — collecting, tagging, recording — matter more than sudden genius
He was simply born brilliant; the butterflies were a coincidence
Winning science fairs is the single event that creates scientists
A famous mentor discovered him and did the real work
discovery.answer: Sustained curiosity plus real research habits — collecting, tagging, recording — matter more than sudden genius
discovery.hook: Ebright didn't start with a laboratory — he started with a net, a notebook and a mother who fed his curiosity. Scientists are trained by habits, not born with titles.

c10_engl_ch15.mission: Follow a butterfly collector from childhood tagging projects to science-fair failures and finally to a real theory about cell life — and pinpoint the exact habits that carried him there.
c10_engl_ch15.finale: The boy who chased monarchs learned the scientist's real secret: curiosity plus stubborn recording beats raw talent that never gets exercised.
c10_engl_ch15.subtitle: Trace how a butterfly hobby became real science
c10_engl_ch15.role: a biographer reconstructing a scientist's childhood
c10_engl_ch15.intro: Before he published research on how cells work, Richard Ebright was a boy in a small town with jars of butterflies and a mother who refused to let him be bored.
c10_engl_ch15.goal: Show that scientific achievement grows from curiosity, discipline and mentorship — not from lone genius.

discovery.question: Matilda Loisel borrows a dazzling diamond necklace for one grand ball, loses it, and spends ten brutal years in poverty paying off the replacement — only to learn the original was fake, worth almost nothing. What is the cruellest irony here?
options: She destroyed her real life to pay for an imitation of the life she dreamed about
Her friend secretly knew it was fake all along
The replacement necklace was also fake, so she was cheated twice
The ball ticket itself was counterfeit
discovery.answer: She destroyed her real life to pay for an imitation of the life she dreamed about
discovery.hook: Matilda's tragedy wasn't losing a necklace — it was that shame stopped her from simply confessing. One honest sentence at the ball would have saved ten years.

c10_engl_ch16.mission: Live one glittering evening on borrowed jewellery, then navigate the decade of debt that follows — and find the exact moment where honesty would have changed everything.
c10_engl_ch16.finale: Ten years of scrubbing floors bought a necklace nobody needed, replacing one that was glass. Vanity wrote the bill; honesty could have torn it up.
c10_engl_ch16.subtitle: Pay for one night of glamour with ten years of poverty
c10_engl_ch16.role: a clerk's wife who longs for the rich life
c10_engl_ch16.intro: You are Matilda: pretty, born for luxury, married to a clerk. An invitation to the Minister's ball should be a dream — except you have nothing to wear. Your friend lends you diamonds. Then, somewhere in the night, they vanish.
c10_engl_ch16.goal: Examine how pride and the fear of shame turn a small accident into a life's catastrophe.

discovery.question: Sulekha — called 'Bholi' (simpleton) after a fall injured her brain and smallpox scarred her face — is the neglected, stammering daughter everyone mocks. At her own wedding, she refuses to marry the groom when he demands dowry money. What made the 'simpleton' suddenly fearless?
options: Schooling — education gave her self-respect, words, and the courage to judge right from wrong
A hidden inheritance made her financially independent
Her father finally stood up for her first
The village elders ordered her to refuse
discovery.answer: Schooling — education gave her self-respect, words, and the courage to judge right from wrong
discovery.hook: The girl who couldn't finish a sentence without stammering delivered the story's most complete sentence: 'No.' Education didn't just teach her to read — it taught her she mattered.

c10_engl_ch17.mission: Grow up as the daughter nobody wants — scarred, stammering, mocked — then let a patient teacher rebuild you word by word until you can refuse an unjust marriage in front of the whole village.
c10_engl_ch17.finale: They named her Bholi to mean 'simple.' School renamed her Sulekha — a girl who could speak, judge, and say no to a greedy bridegroom.
c10_engl_ch17.subtitle: Watch a mocked girl find the one word that changes her life
c10_engl_ch17.role: a neglected child discovering her own voice
c10_engl_ch17.intro: Everyone in the village calls you Bholi — the simpleton who fell off a cot, survived smallpox, and can barely speak. Then the new school opens, and a teacher speaks to you as if you are a person.
c10_engl_ch17.goal: Show how education and one caring teacher transform neglect into self-respect and moral courage.

discovery.question: In 2040, Martian invaders land on Earth to conquer it — but flee in terror after 'decoding' a book of nursery rhymes, convinced that Earthlings have explosive weapons and interstellar reach. How did a children's book defeat an invasion?
options: The Martians misread rhymes as military intelligence — 'Humpty Dumpty' proved Earth's violent power
The rhymes contained a hidden code planted by Earth's scientists
The book emitted radiation that poisoned the Martian fleet
The Historian hypnotised the invaders through the museum display
discovery.answer: The Martians misread rhymes as military intelligence — 'Humpty Dumpty' proved Earth's violent power
discovery.hook: The Martians were defeated by their own arrogance: they 'translated' Mother Goose into a weapons manual. A book only 'saves the Earth' because the invaders couldn't imagine being wrong.

c10_engl_ch18.mission: Command a Martian space fleet invading a library, assign 'experts' to decode a mysterious Earth book — and watch your mighty armada retreat before Mother Goose.
c10_engl_ch18.finale: The invasion failed not with a bang but with a nursery rhyme. Superior technology lost to a superior imagination — Earth's, and the playwright's.
c10_engl_ch18.subtitle: Repel a Martian invasion with nothing but nursery rhymes
c10_engl_ch18.role: a Martian fleet commander decoding Earth's secrets
c10_engl_ch18.intro: The year is 2040. Your fleet lands at a strange Earth building called a 'library' — a warehouse of primitive 'books.' Somewhere in those paper rectangles must be the secret of this planet's power.
c10_engl_ch18.goal: See how satire uses dramatic irony: the 'backward' humans win because the 'advanced' invaders cannot read without arrogance.

discovery.question: A river flows through a remote valley. To a city engineer it's a hydroelectric resource; to a village upstream it's irrigation; to an untouched forest stretch, the same water is 'not yet a resource.' How can one substance switch between being and not being a resource?
options: A substance becomes a resource only when it meets a need AND is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable
Resources are fixed by nature — the engineer is simply wrong
Anything wet counts as a water resource automatically
Only things that can be sold in markets are resources
discovery.answer: A substance becomes a resource only when it meets a need AND is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable
discovery.hook: A rock in a desert isn't a resource until technology, demand and cost line up. 'Resource' is a relationship between humans and nature — not a label stamped on objects.

c10_geo_ch01.mission: Audit a patch of land — soil, water, forests, minerals, sunlight — and sort each item into biotic, abiotic, renewable, non-renewable and 'not yet a resource,' then defend each call.
c10_geo_ch01.finale: Everything around you is either a resource or a resource-in-waiting. What decides isn't the thing itself — it's human need, technology and wisdom.
c10_geo_ch01.subtitle: Decide what counts as a resource — and what doesn't yet
c10_geo_ch01.role: a resource planner surveying a valley
c10_geo_ch01.intro: You've been handed a map of a district and one blunt question: what here is actually a resource? The answer turns out to be trickier than 'everything useful.'
c10_geo_ch01.goal: Classify resources by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and development status — and explain why the same substance can shift categories.

discovery.question: India holds over 47,000 plant and 89,000 animal species, yet a single town's new highway can erase species that took millions of years to evolve. Conservationists argue even 'useless' insects deserve protection. What's the strongest reason?
options: Every species is a link in an ecological web — losing unknown ones can collapse services like pollination and soil renewal that we depend on
Rare species are always worth money as tourist attractions
Laws require it, so the debate is already settled
Insects pollinate every single crop humans eat
discovery.answer: Every species is a link in an ecological web — losing unknown ones can collapse services like pollination and soil renewal that we depend on
discovery.hook: You can't pull threads out of a web and promise it will hold. We protect species we've never named because ecosystems don't publish their load-bearing walls.

c10_geo_ch02.mission: Map India's wild wealth — from Himalayan rhododendrons to Western Ghats frogs — rank the threats pushing species toward extinction, and choose which conservation strategies actually work.
c10_geo_ch02.finale: Forests aren't just timber and tigers aren't just mascots. Biodiversity is the country's insurance policy — and we keep cancelling it.
c10_geo_ch02.subtitle: Defend species you've never heard of before they vanish
c10_geo_ch02.intro: India is one of only 17 mega-diverse countries on Earth. Your job: decide where the next highway, dam or mine goes — knowing every 'empty' patch of forest is full of lives.
c10_geo_ch02.goal: Connect India's relief, climate and soil to its biodiversity, weigh depletion causes, and evaluate conservation from Project Tiger to sacred groves.

discovery.question: Bengaluru gets decent monsoon rain and sits near rivers, yet apartment blocks there queue for water tankers. Meanwhile some genuinely dry regions manage fine. How can a water-rich place run out of water?
options: Scarcity can be economic, not just physical — poor infrastructure, pollution and over-extraction can make available water unusable or unreachable
Tanker mafias secretly export the city's water at night
Rain in cities instantly evaporates before touching the ground
Rivers legally belong only to the states they originate in
discovery.answer: Scarcity can be economic, not just physical — poor infrastructure, pollution and over-extraction can make available water unusable or unreachable
discovery.hook: Running out of water isn't only about rain — a city can stand beside a river and still thirst if the water is polluted, over-pumped or never harvested.

c10_geo_ch03.mission: Investigate why a rain-blessed city still buys tanker water: trace over-exploited aquifers, polluted rivers and missing storage, then design a fix using dams and rooftop harvesting wisely.
c10_geo_ch03.finale: Freshwater is renewable but not infinite. The crisis isn't that the sky forgot us — it's that we paved the catchments, poisoned the rivers and pumped the aquifers dry.
c10_geo_ch03.subtitle: Solve why a wet city still runs dry
c10_geo_ch03.intro: Three-fourths of Earth's surface is water, yet your city's taps run at fixed hours. Your task is to find where the water actually goes — and why 'enough' on paper means scarcity in pipes.
c10_geo_ch03.goal: Separate physical from economic scarcity, weigh the promises and costs of multipurpose dams, and make the case for rainwater harvesting.

discovery.question: Agriculture employs about 43% of India's workers but produces only around 18% of the country's GVA. If farming is so 'unproductive,' why can't India simply shift those workers into factories and services?
options: Agriculture also feeds the nation, supplies raw material to industries and earns export income — and manufacturing can't absorb that many workers quickly
It actually can — economists just refuse to admit it
Farm workers refuse all other jobs by tradition alone
The 18% figure is a data error; farms produce most of GDP
discovery.answer: Agriculture also feeds the nation, supplies raw material to industries and earns export income — and manufacturing can't absorb that many workers quickly
discovery.hook: A sector can shrink in GDP share while its importance grows — your breakfast, your cotton shirt and India's rice exports all start in a field.

c10_geo_ch04.mission: Follow one grain of wheat through India's farm economy: choose between subsistence and commercial farming logic, match crops to soils and seasons, and judge which reforms actually help the farmer.
c10_geo_ch04.finale: Two in five Indians work the land to feed all of us. Agriculture's share of GDP fell — its responsibility never did.
c10_geo_ch04.subtitle: Run the sector that feeds a billion on a fifth of the economy
c10_geo_ch04.intro: Nearly half of India's workers still farm, yet farming earns less than a fifth of the national income. Somewhere between the field and the GDP figure lies the real story of Indian agriculture.
c10_geo_ch04.goal: Weigh agriculture's true economic roles — employment, food security, raw materials, exports — and understand farming types, cropping seasons and reform debates.

discovery.question: The iron in your bike, the mica in old electricals, the salt in the sea — all minerals, all 'dug up.' Yet geologists say minerals are a 'one-time inheritance': once mined, they're gone. If minerals form naturally, why can't the Earth just make more?
options: They form over geological timescales of millions of years — trivially renewable to Earth, effectively non-renewable to us
Mining permanently stops all mineral formation worldwide
Earth does make them fast, but companies hide new deposits
Only metals are finite; other minerals regrow like forests
discovery.answer: They form over geological timescales of millions of years — trivially renewable to Earth, effectively non-renewable to us
discovery.hook: Earth IS making more minerals right now — it just works on a clock of millions of years while we mine on a clock of decades. Finite isn't about geology; it's about timescale.

c10_geo_ch05.mission: Hunt India's minerals from veins and lodes to alluvial sands: classify metallic and non-metallic finds, place iron ore and bauxite belts on the map, then decide how to use a finite inheritance.
c10_geo_ch05.finale: Every mineral you use was made once and will never be remade in human time. Conservation isn't green idealism here — it's arithmetic.
c10_geo_ch05.subtitle: Spend a one-time geological inheritance wisely
c10_geo_ch05.intro: Under India's soils lies a portfolio millions of years in the making — iron, manganese, bauxite, mica, coal. Your job is to find it, classify it, and explain why 'we'll just find more' is a dangerous plan.
c10_geo_ch05.goal: Define minerals, master their modes of occurrence and Indian distribution, and argue for conservation of an effectively non-renewable endowment.

discovery.question: Early cotton textile mills clustered almost entirely around Mumbai and Ahmedabad — not near India's biggest cities or cotton's fanciest markets. What pulled an entire industry to that one coastal belt?
options: A convergence of location factors: nearby raw cotton, moist coastal air for spinning, ports, cheap labour, capital and a big market
The British legally banned textile mills everywhere else
Cotton only grows within 100 km of the sea
Mumbai had the country's only electricity supply then
discovery.answer: A convergence of location factors: nearby raw cotton, moist coastal air for spinning, ports, cheap labour, capital and a big market
discovery.hook: Industries aren't planted randomly — they migrate to wherever raw material, labour, power, transport and markets add up to the lowest cost. Geography is arithmetic with a map.

c10_geo_ch06.mission: Site a new factory from scratch: weigh raw material, labour, power, capital, transport, market and government policy for competing locations, then defend why industry also means pollution.
c10_geo_ch06.finale: Manufacturing turns harvests into incomes and ores into machines — the sector that decides whether India stays a supplier of raw stuff or becomes a maker.
c10_geo_ch06.subtitle: Pick the perfect spot for a factory — then pay the true price
c10_geo_ch06.intro: A company hands you a map of India and asks: where do we build? The honest answer involves cotton fields, coal seams, railway lines, crowded markets — and the smoke that follows.
c10_geo_ch06.goal: Explain manufacturing's role in the economy, apply the seven industrial location factors to real cases, and confront industry's environmental costs.

discovery.question: India has roads, railways, waterways, airways and even pipelines. A fisherman's catch, a software engineer's commute and crude oil bound for a refinery all travel differently — yet the chapter calls ALL of them 'lifelines.' What makes a mode of transport earn that title?
options: It links production centres with consumption centres — moving goods, people and services so the economy actually functions
It must be government-owned and nationally funded
Only modes that cross state borders count as lifelines
It must carry passengers, not just cargo
discovery.answer: It links production centres with consumption centres — moving goods, people and services so the economy actually functions
discovery.hook: A mango that can't reach a market is just a falling fruit. Transport is what turns geography into an economy — every mode is a different kind of vein in the same body.

c10_geo_ch07.mission: Route a week of Indian life — farm produce to mandis, coal to power plants, crude through pipelines, passengers by rail and air — and match each cargo to the mode that fits it best.
c10_geo_ch07.finale: Roads knit villages to towns, rails move the bulk, pipes flow invisibly underground. Together they are why a country this size behaves like one economy.
c10_geo_ch07.subtitle: Move a nation's goods across five kinds of lifelines
c10_geo_ch07.intro: A fish caught in Kerala, a passenger flying to Delhi, gas flowing under Gujarat — all of it is transport doing one job: connecting where things are made to where they are needed.
c10_geo_ch07.goal: Compare the five modes of transport and communication in India, and explain why each earns the title 'lifeline of the national economy.'

discovery.question: Before 1789, a Frenchman's loyalty belonged to his king and his region. After the Revolution, he was a 'citoyen' of 'la patrie' — saluting a tricolour and singing the Marseillaise. What did the Revolution actually invent?
options: The idea of the nation: a community of equal citizens bound by shared rights and symbols, not by obedience to a monarch
The world's first written constitution anywhere in history
Voting rights for every adult including women and the poor
The French language itself as a tool of unity
discovery.answer: The idea of the nation: a community of equal citizens bound by shared rights and symbols, not by obedience to a monarch
discovery.hook: Kings ruled subjects; nations are made of citizens. France didn't just change rulers in 1789 — it changed what people felt they belonged to.

c10_hist_ch01.mission: Watch Europe redraw itself: track how one revolution's ideas of nation and citizenship spread, collide with empires, and forge Germany and Italy out of dozens of fragments.
c10_hist_ch01.finale: A flag, an anthem, uniform laws — nationalism was manufactured as deliberately as any machine. Europe spent a century living with the consequences.
c10_hist_ch01.subtitle: Follow one idea as it remade a whole continent's map
c10_hist_ch01.role: a correspondent tracing revolutions across 19th-century Europe
c10_hist_ch01.intro: In 1789 Paris crowds stormed a fortress and invented a new political word: citizen. Within decades, students in secret societies, artists painting allegories, and revolutionaries like Mazzini and Garibaldi were all chasing the same idea.
c10_hist_ch01.goal: Explain how the French Revolution birthed nationalism, how it spread through Europe, and how culture and revolution together unified Germany and Italy.

discovery.question: During the First World War, India sent soldiers, money and supplies for Britain, and Britain hinted at self-rule in return. Right after the war, Indians got the Rowlatt Act — detention without trial. What did this betrayal prove to Indian nationalists?
options: Loyalty and petitions wouldn't win freedom — only mass mobilisation would, setting the stage for Gandhi's movements
Britain had always planned to leave India by 1920 anyway
Indians should have supported the Central Powers instead
The Rowlatt Act was a printing error quickly withdrawn
discovery.answer: Loyalty and petitions wouldn't win freedom — only mass mobilisation would, setting the stage for Gandhi's movements
discovery.hook: India paid for the war in soldiers and taxes, and was repaid with a law that jailed dissent without trial. The mask slipped — and nationalism shifted from drawing rooms to the streets.

c10_hist_ch02.mission: Relive 1915–1947's turning points: from the Rowlatt Act's betrayal through Jallianwala Bagh, the salt march and Quit India — and feel how a subject population became a movement.
c10_hist_ch02.finale: Nationalism in India wasn't born in a conference hall — it was forged by broken promises, a massacre in a walled garden, and a 240-mile walk to make salt.
c10_hist_ch02.subtitle: March from loyalty to mass rebellion in thirty turbulent years
c10_hist_ch02.role: a young Indian deciding whether to join the freedom struggle
c10_hist_ch02.intro: You grew up hearing that loyalty to the Empire would earn India its due. Then came wartime taxes, the Rowlatt Act, and the sound of firing at Jallianwala Bagh — and a thin man with a staff asking you to march for salt.
c10_hist_ch02.goal: Connect wartime hardship to the rise of Gandhian mass movements and explain how each phase — Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India — widened the struggle.

discovery.question: Long before airplanes or the internet, Chinese silk reached Rome, Buddhism walked into China, and the humble potato crossed an ocean to change Indian kitchens forever. What made all this movement possible centuries ago?
options: The Silk Routes — a shifting network of land and sea paths carrying goods, religions, technologies and even diseases across Afro-Eurasia
A single paved highway built by one empire from China to Rome
Viking longships that traded directly with India
Camel post offices that delivered parcels door to door
discovery.answer: The Silk Routes — a shifting network of land and sea paths carrying goods, religions, technologies and even diseases across Afro-Eurasia
discovery.hook: The 'Silk Road' was never one road and carried far more than silk — faiths, gunpowder, paper, plagues. Globalisation didn't start with the internet; it started with caravans and monsoon winds.

c10_hist_ch03.mission: Travel three thousand years of connection: ride the Silk Routes, sail with the monsoon winds, watch the Americas feed and plague the Old World, and see how indenture rebuilt empire's workforce.
c10_hist_ch03.finale: The global world wasn't discovered in 1492 — it was stitched together by traders, monks, sailors and slaves long before. Columbus just changed the stitching.
c10_hist_ch03.subtitle: Trace how trade, food and disease built one connected world
c10_hist_ch03.role: a trader's apprentice crossing ancient routes
c10_hist_ch03.intro: Your caravan carries silk and spices, but the real cargo is invisible — ideas, faiths and microbes hitching a ride. You are travelling the network that made the world global centuries before the word existed.
c10_hist_ch03.goal: Understand the Silk Routes, the Columbian Exchange, and how trade, migration and disease forged the modern global world.

discovery.question: Decades before steam factories roared, European merchants were already organising mass production — in peasant cottages. Farm families wove cloth at home with merchant-supplied yarn between harvest seasons. Why did merchants choose cottages over factories?
options: It was proto-industrialisation: cheap rural labour with idle seasons let merchants produce for distant markets without building factories or fighting guilds
Peasants were legally forbidden from entering towns
Factories hadn't been invented anywhere in the world yet
Cottage cloth was always higher quality than machine cloth
discovery.answer: It was proto-industrialisation: cheap rural labour with idle seasons let merchants produce for distant markets without building factories or fighting guilds
discovery.hook: Industrialisation didn't begin with the factory whistle — it began quietly in farmhouses, where a loom sat beside the kitchen and a merchant's cart collected the finished cloth.

c10_hist_ch04.mission: Follow cloth through the industrial revolution: from peasant cottages under the putting-out system to Manchester's steam mills — and then to colonial India, where Indian weavers met machine competition.
c10_hist_ch04.finale: The factory didn't invent industrial labour; it reorganised it. And when machines outproduced hands, entire artisan worlds — including India's — paid the price.
c10_hist_ch04.subtitle: Watch production move from farmhouse loom to steam-powered mill
c10_hist_ch04.role: a merchant's agent turned industrial-age observer
c10_hist_ch04.intro: You supply yarn to cottage weavers across the countryside — until one day a smoky brick building with a steam engine outproduces a hundred villages. Industrialisation has arrived, and nothing stays the same.
c10_hist_ch04.goal: Explain proto-industrialisation, the rise of factories, and how industrialisation transformed both Britain and colonial India.

discovery.question: The world's oldest dated printed book — the Diamond Sutra, 868 CE — was made in China by carving text into wooden blocks, centuries before Gutenberg. If printing was this old, why did it take so long to change the world?
options: Woodblock printing was slow and craft-bound; only cheap paper, movable type and mass literacy turned print into a revolution
China kept the technique a total state secret until 1900
Ancient people simply had nothing worth printing
Woodblocks could only print pictures, never words
