discovery.question: Two sequences both start 2, 4 — but one goes 8, 16, 32 and the other 6, 8, 10. Same start, wildly different futures. What's the invisible difference?
options: One multiplies by 2 each step (2ⁿ — exponential growth), the other adds 2 each step (2n — linear growth); multiplying explodes past adding
Nothing — they'll meet again later
One is prime numbers, one is even
The second sequence made an arithmetic error
discovery.answer: One multiplies by 2 each step (2ⁿ — exponential growth), the other adds 2 each step (2n — linear growth); multiplying explodes past adding
discovery.hook: A sequence is a function wearing a disguise: each term is pinned to its position number n, and the first term is n=1 — never n=0. For aₙ = n² − 1, the sequence starts at 0 (1² − 1), not −1.

c9_math_ch08.mission: Crack position rules: generate terms of aₙ = (2n+1)/n term by term, tell a true sequence from a mere set, and settle why '1, 3, 5, 7, 9' is finite even though you could keep adding 2 forever.
c9_math_ch08.finale: A sequence is an ordered list wired to position: term 1, term 2, term n. Find the rule aₙ and the whole infinite pattern is yours — and whether it adds or multiplies decides whether it crawls or explodes.
c9_math_ch08.subtitle: Every term knows its position
c9_math_ch08.intro: ₹10 in week 1, ₹20 in week 2, ₹30 in week 3 — your savings are secretly a sequence. Learn to read the rule hiding inside any list of numbers.
c9_math_ch08.goal: Understand sequences as ordered, position-indexed lists — writing terms from rules like aₙ = 2n+1, distinguishing finite/infinite, and comparing additive vs multiplicative growth.

discovery.question: A student meticulously records which colour shirt they wear on 'lucky' exam days for a whole month — neat table, perfect order. Is that science?
options: No — personal tidiness isn't science; a claim must be falsifiable, controlled and checked by others, which 'lucky shirt' tracking never does
Yes — systematic recording is science
Yes — if the data is accurate enough
No — only lab coats count as science
discovery.answer: No — personal tidiness isn't science; a claim must be falsifiable, controlled and checked by others, which 'lucky shirt' tracking never does
discovery.hook: A scientific 'theory' is the opposite of a guess — it's the highest-status, most-tested explanation there is. And science never 'proves' anything true; it survives by failing to be falsified, one reproducible test at a time.

c9_physics_ch01.mission: Run a WhatsApp forward — 'NASA confirms lemon on forehead cures migraine instantly' — through the gauntlet: is it falsifiable, peer-reviewed, reproducible? Then turn a home superstition into a controlled, testable investigation.
c9_physics_ch01.finale: Science is systematic because it's communally verified: falsifiable claims, controlled tests, results anyone can replicate. Observing something many times isn't enough — Grandma's tulsi cure still needs a placebo group.
c9_physics_ch01.subtitle: Why 'I saw it work' isn't enough
c9_physics_ch01.role: a claim-checker for the internet age
c9_physics_ch01.intro: Every day, forwards and family wisdom make claims about the world. Your job: tell which ones could survive a real scientific test — and which crumble the moment controls appear.
c9_physics_ch01.goal: Distinguish scientific from non-scientific claims using falsifiability, controls, reproducibility and peer review — and understand science as communally verified knowledge.

discovery.question: You walk a full lap around a circular track and stop exactly where you started. How far did you 'move'?
options: Distance = the whole circumference, but displacement = zero — the straight line from start to end has no length
Both are the circumference
Both are zero — you ended where you began
Displacement is the circumference, distance is zero
discovery.answer: Distance = the whole circumference, but displacement = zero — the straight line from start to end has no length
discovery.hook: Distance counts every step; displacement only asks 'where did you end up versus where you began?' Walk 10 m forward and 10 m back: distance is 20 m, displacement is 0. Distance is always ≥ displacement's size.

c9_physics_ch02.mission: Track a car going 50 m east then 30 m west, a cyclist going 3 km north then 4 km east (Pythagoras gives the shortcut), and a particle bouncing along a number line — computing both distance and displacement each time.
c9_physics_ch02.finale: Distance is the odometer — it adds every metre you travel. Displacement is the crow's flight — the straight arrow from start to finish, direction included. Same units, totally different questions.
c9_physics_ch02.subtitle: Every step counts vs. only the endpoints
c9_physics_ch02.intro: A delivery scooter zigs and zags all day — its odometer tells one story, its 'how far from home' arrow tells another. Learn to compute both and never mix them up.
c9_physics_ch02.goal: Distinguish distance (scalar path length) from displacement (vector start-to-end) — calculating both for multi-segment motion and explaining why distance ≥ |displacement|.

discovery.question: A spacecraft in deep space coasts at 10,000 m/s with its engines off. What happens to it?
options: It keeps going at 10,000 m/s forever — no force acts on it, so nothing changes its velocity
It gradually slows down and stops
It speeds up — no air to hold it back
It drifts sideways eventually
discovery.answer: It keeps going at 10,000 m/s forever — no force acts on it, so nothing changes its velocity
discovery.hook: Force isn't needed to KEEP moving — only to change motion. Everyday things stop because friction secretly pushes back. And inertia is just mass being stubborn: a heavy table resists starting AND stopping more than a light chair.

c9_physics_ch03.mission: Explain the lurch: why passengers pitch forward in a braking car (inertia of motion), why the book on the table never starts itself (inertia of rest), and why a hockey puck on ice outslides the same puck on grass.
c9_physics_ch03.finale: Newton's First Law: a body keeps doing exactly what it's doing — resting or cruising straight — until an unbalanced force interferes. Forces change motion; they don't create it.
c9_physics_ch03.subtitle: Nothing stops unless something stops it
c9_physics_ch03.intro: Why does your body slam forward when the bus brakes, and why does a book just sit there? One law explains both — inertia, the universe's resistance to change.
c9_physics_ch03.goal: Understand Newton's First Law — bodies resist changes in rest or uniform motion (inertia, measured by mass) — and that force changes motion rather than maintaining it.

discovery.question: You hold a heavy schoolbag perfectly still for a full minute — arms burning, sweating, exhausted. How much work did physics say you did?
options: Zero joules — work needs force AND displacement; a bag that doesn't move gets no work done on it, however tired you feel
Lots — your muscles clearly burned energy
Force × 60 seconds
Half the bag's weight in joules
discovery.answer: Zero joules — work needs force AND displacement; a bag that doesn't move gets no work done on it, however tired you feel
discovery.hook: Your tired muscles and physics disagree: work = force × displacement, and no displacement means zero joules. Bonus trap: a coolie walking 100 m with a load does zero work AGAINST gravity — the force points down, the motion points sideways.

c9_physics_ch04.mission: Calculate the joules: a farmer pushing a cart 25 m at 120 N, two students pushing identical boxes different distances — then catch the exam trap where a box's weight gets mistaken for the pushing force.
c9_physics_ch04.finale: W = F × s: force times displacement in the force's direction, measured in joules. Effort without movement earns applause but zero joules — physics only pays for distance covered.
c9_physics_ch04.subtitle: Force alone doesn't count — things must move
c9_physics_ch04.intro: Pushing a desk 3 metres? Work. Holding a suitcase still while your arms shake? Zero work. Learn the strict physics definition and spot every impostor.
c9_physics_ch04.goal: Understand work as W = Fs — requiring both force and displacement in the same direction — and identify zero-work and perpendicular-force situations.

discovery.question: Strike a steel thali, then press your palm flat on it — the sound dies instantly. The plate is still there, still struck. What did your hand actually kill?
options: The vibration — sound only exists while something oscillates; stop the to-and-fro motion and no compressions reach the air
The echo — sound needs to bounce
The metal's sound supply ran out
Your hand absorbed the noise particles
discovery.answer: The vibration — sound only exists while something oscillates; stop the to-and-fro motion and no compressions reach the air
discovery.hook: Every instrument hides a different vibrator: sitar = string, tabla = membrane, flute = air column, bell = solid plate, your voice = vocal cords. And hitting harder raises loudness (amplitude), never the pitch (frequency).

c9_physics_ch05.mission: Go vibration-hunting: feel your throat hum 'Om', identify the vibrating part in five Indian instruments, and build the spoon-and-thread trick that proves sound rides solids better than air.
c9_physics_ch05.finale: No vibration, no sound — every note you've ever heard is matter oscillating and shoving air into waves of squeezes and stretches. Silence is just stillness.
c9_physics_ch05.subtitle: Every sound is something shaking
c9_physics_ch05.intro: From a humming throat to a temple bell, every sound traces back to one thing: a vibration. Hunt down the vibrator inside each instrument and catch the wave it throws into the air.
c9_physics_ch05.goal: Understand that sound is produced by vibrating objects creating compressions and rarefactions — and identify the vibrating source in strings, membranes, air columns and plates.

discovery.question: Earth is closest to the Sun in January — yet that's when the Northern Hemisphere freezes through winter. If distance controlled the seasons, shouldn't January be the warmest?
options: No — the 23.5° axial tilt wins: the hemisphere tilted away gets slanted rays spread thin over more area, no matter the small distance change
Yes — it should be warmer; the seasons are broken
The calendar is misaligned with the Sun
January is actually Earth's farthest point
discovery.answer: No — the 23.5° axial tilt wins: the hemisphere tilted away gets slanted rays spread thin over more area, no matter the small distance change
discovery.hook: Slant is everything: the same sunbeam covering 1 m² at the equator spreads across ~2 m² at 60° latitude, halving the heating. And in June, the far north's 18-hour days can out-collect the equator's intense noon — day length can beat ray angle.

c9_physics_ch06.mission: Quantify the slant: use insolation = solar constant × cos(zenith angle) to find noon heating at 45°, prove why poles stay cold, and test whether 60°N's endless June day really beats the equator's blazing noon.
c9_physics_ch06.finale: It's not how far the Sun is — it's how squarely its rays hit. Spherical geometry, axial tilt and day length together decide who bakes and who freezes, driving every wind and current on Earth.
c9_physics_ch06.subtitle: Why the poles freeze and the equator bakes
c9_physics_ch06.intro: Same Sun, same planet — wildly different heating. Follow one sunbeam from equator to pole and watch it stretch thin, and discover the cosine rule that runs Earth's entire climate engine.
c9_physics_ch06.goal: Explain uneven solar heating — angle of incidence, area spread, atmospheric path and day length — driven by Earth's spherical shape and 23.5° axial tilt.
